title: That's how it is every day
goal: Talk about habits and general truths with the aorist *-ir*, and use it for polite requests.
bekal: telling habits (*-ir*) apart from what's happening now (*-yor*)
asking for something politely: *bir çay alır mısınız?*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mutfakta sohbet
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning. Fatma Hanım is making breakfast; Budi is helping slice tomatoes.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.id: Budi, what do you usually do in the mornings?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Genellikle erken kalkarım, sonra biraz Türkçe çalışırım.
lines.id: I usually get up early, then study a little Turkish.
lines.literal: usually early get-up-I, then a-little Turkish-language work-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Sometimes. In Indonesia we usually eat rice.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.id: Rice first thing in the morning? I don't believe it!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Gerçek! Peki Türkler kahvaltıda ne yer?
lines.id: It's true! So what do Turks eat for breakfast?
lines.literal: true! well Turk-s breakfast-at what eat?

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Peynir, zeytin, domates, ekmek. Ve tabii çay içeriz.
lines.id: Cheese, olives, tomatoes, bread. And of course we drink tea.
lines.literal: cheese, olive, tomato, bread. and of-course tea drink-we.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How many glasses of tea do you drink a day?

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Ben mi? On, on beş. Az içerim!
lines.id: Me? Ten, fifteen. I drink very little!
lines.literal: I question? ten, ten five. little drink-I!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Az mı?! Ben günde iki içerim, yeter.
lines.id: Little?! I drink two a day, and that's enough.
lines.literal: little question?! I day-in two drink-I, enough.

lines.speaker: Fatma:
lines.text: Alışırsın. Herkes alışır. Bir bardak daha alır mısın?
lines.id: You'll get used to it. Everyone does. Will you have another glass?
lines.literal: get-used-you. everyone gets-used. one glass more take question-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Of course I will. Thank you for the food!

notes: **Sabahları means "in the mornings", not "early in the morning".** The plural + *-ı* on a time word turns it into a habit: *sabahları*, *akşamları*, *pazartesileri*, *kışları*. This form always pairs with an *-ir* verb.
**İnanmam is a negative, not a typo.** The aorist has its own negative that doesn't follow any other pattern: *ben* takes *-mem/-mam*, *biz* takes *-meyiz/-mayız*. Everyone else takes *-mez/-maz*.

**Alır mısın? is a polite way to offer.** The aorist is used for gentle requests, much like "would you ..." in English. *Kapıyı kapatır mısın?* (would you close the door?), *Bir dakika bekler misiniz?* (could you wait a moment?).

**In Turkey, tea isn't measured in cups but in *ince belli bardak*** — small tulip-shaped glasses. Fifteen glasses a day is no joke: Turkey drinks more tea per person than any other country in the world.

blocks.text: The form Turks call *geniş zaman* — "broad time" — is used for things that are **always, usually or basically** true. It's not a specific time; it's time without limits.

blocks.text: Thirteen one-syllable verbs rebel and take *-ir* instead of *-er*. They're all very common words, so you'll pick them up without trying:
This is the one place in all of Turkish that really has to be memorized separately. The negative of *geniş zaman* doesn't use *-ir* at all:
For stems with back vowels, the forms are *-mam*, *-mazsın*, *-maz*, *-mayız*, *-mazsınız*, *-mazlar*: *yapmam*, *anlamaz*, *çalışmayız*.

blocks.title: Olmaz — a word you'll hear every day
items: *Olmaz* is the *geniş zaman* negative of *olmak*, and it means "can't, not allowed, no way". It turns down offers, prices, ideas and plans.
Its partner is *olur* — "fine, OK, sure". These two words are the yes and no buttons of everyday Turkish life, and you've been using them since unit 9 without knowing the form.

head: Aorist -ir
-yor form
The difference
rows: general truth / the water is boiling
I'll come if needed / definitely coming

blocks.text: The subtlest difference is in the last row. *Yarın gelirim* sounds like willingness ("I can come tomorrow"), while *yarın geliyorum* is a settled plan. For a binding promise, Turks choose *-ecek*: *yarın geleceğim*.

blocks.title: Adverbs that call for -ir
items: Some words almost always pair with the aorist: *her gün*, *her zaman*, *genellikle*, *bazen*, *hiç*, *sık sık* (often), *nadiren* (rarely), *asla* (never ever).
If one of these words shows up in your sentence, the verb is almost certainly *-ir*, not *-yor*.

blocks.title: Unit 11 review
items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild these from memory: "What did you do yesterday?" · "I went to Sultanahmet." · "Did you see Hagia Sophia?" · "I was very tired yesterday." · "Then I came back by ferry."
Then put these into the past: *geliyorum*, *yapıyorsun*, *görüyor*, *yorgunum*.

exercises.prompt: Make it negative (watch out for the special form).
Choose the right form: *-ir* or *-yor*. Write the full sentence.
Put the words in the right order.
